segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By Tuesday morning Mrs Hale had two pieces of news and one counter to tell them at, and she was seen to begin three times and change her mind twice.

segments.speaker: Mrs Hale
segments.text: The estate is to fit the east wing for a school. Floor, glazing and a stove, and a man coming from Alresford on the twentieth to measure it. And the curate is to marry Miss Vane. No. The curate is to marry Miss Vane, and the estate is to fit the east wing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She settled at last on giving them together, which pleased nobody, since a parish likes to be astonished twice.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mrs Pike had no such difficulty. She had the whole of it arranged in her own account before the coach had gone out again.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: Where do you suppose Miss Marchmont heard of that cracked beam at all? At my dinner. And where do you suppose Mr Rowe first sat down in a room with Miss Vane and could not think of a word to say to her? At my dinner. A schoolroom and a wedding, and not one of you would believe me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Mrs Pike, on her own doorstep, to the sexton. Nobody troubled to correct her. Judith had in fact said it on the step, waiting for the lantern, and the step belonged to Mrs Pike.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Miss Marchmont went up on the Friday coach with her boxes and a roll of measurements. She had got her uncle's promise in writing, and she had got it in a fortnight, and she was not modest about either.

segments.speaker: Miss Louisa Marchmont
segments.text: Write to me. Not about the weather, and not about who is engaged, because I shall know. Write and tell me whether the stove smokes, because his man swears it will not and I do not believe him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Miss Marchmont, from the step of the coach.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: I will. And here is something to be going on with.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judith gave her the list of six books made out for Mrs Cobbe in October, copied fair, with the shelf numbers against them.

segments.speaker: Miss Louisa Marchmont
segments.text: Is the orphan in it?

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: She is not. I have some standards.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mrs Hale watched the coach out and reported that Miss Marchmont had read the whole way to the turn without once looking up, which was thought very odd of her.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mr Rowe came to the apothecary's on the Saturday and was made to stand on the shop side of the counter, among the drawers of chalk and rhubarb.

segments.speaker: Mr Owen Vane
segments.text: You may have her, and I am glad of it, and I shall say so in the Bell so that they hear it from me first. One condition.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Owen.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: Name it.

segments.speaker: Mr Owen Vane
segments.text: You will never again put my sister into a cart without looking at the wheels of it, and if you cannot tell a sound spoke from a split one, you will come and fetch me, and I will look for you.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: I cannot tell a sound spoke from a split one.

segments.speaker: Mr Owen Vane
segments.text: I know it. That is why the condition is worded so.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The banns were read for the first time on the last Sunday in June, and the men were on the east wing roof the same week, stripping the old lead. Fenner came over from Bramdean after all, for the chimney of the stove, and grumbled at being paid out of the estate as though he had not been paid at all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The subscription book was shut with nine shillings entered in it, and a promise of a load of straw. The straw came. Two of the Barrow girls walked up the lane on the Sunday to look at the east wing with its scaffold, and stood at the gate a full quarter of an hour saying nothing much. Mrs Pike stood on her own step in the sun and accepted the thanks of everybody who passed.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: You are all very welcome. And I am not finished.
